prime.problem: The loss is one number, 2.2067, but there are 220 weights. Backprop has to start somewhere, and its first step, through softmax and \(-\ln\), looks like it needs a \(5 \times 5\) table of slopes for every position.
prime.fits: The first backward card. It starts from the loss built on the logits-and-loss card and the softmax from card 7, and hands \(dz\) (\(3 \times 5\)) down to the output head on the next card.
expect: \(dX \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial X}\), the same shape as \(X\)
the softmax Jacobian \(\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j)\)
prime.goal: Derive \(dz[2] = [0.0359,\allowbreak\ 0.0128,\allowbreak\ 0.0155,\allowbreak\ -0.3109,\allowbreak\ 0.2468]\) from \(p\) and the target, check it with a nudge, and explain why frameworks hand logits, not probabilities, to the loss.

attend: The loss reads one probability per row. Through which term does every other logit in the row still pick up a gradient?
Where exactly does the \(1/p\) from \(-\ln\) meet a \(p\) from softmax, and what is left after they cancel?
Why does the right word get pushed by \(1 - p\) while each wrong word gets pushed by its own share?
Why must each row of \(dz\) add to 0, and how is that the same fact as softmax ignoring a shift of the whole row?
What goes wrong in float32 if you compute softmax first and take \(-\ln\) afterwards, and how does \(\text{logsumexp}(z) - z_y\) avoid it?

must: \(L_t = -\ln p[t, y_t]\) → chain rule: \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j} = (-1/p_y) \cdot \frac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_j}\) → softmax Jacobian \(\frac{\partial p_y}{\partial z_j} = p_y(\delta_{yj} - p_j)\) → the \(p_y\) cancels → \(p_j - y_j\) → ÷ 3 for the mean → \(dz[2] = [0.0359,\allowbreak\ 0.0128,\allowbreak\ 0.0155,\allowbreak\ -0.3109,\allowbreak\ 0.2468]\)

Every logit sits in softmax's total → raising a rival's logit lowers \(p_y\) → every wrong word gets a positive gradient equal to its share → a step pushes it down by that share, so the confident wrong mat (0.7404) is pushed hardest, and the right word goes up by \(1 - p = 0.9327\)

\(p\) and \(y\) each add to 1 → each row of \(p - y\) adds to 0 → the gradient has no part along 'shift every logit equally' → matches softmax ignoring a shift (adding 1.0 to row 2 changes the loss by \(0.0\))

\(-\ln\) of softmax \(= \text{logsumexp}(z) - z_y\) → the log undoes the exp → its slope is \(p - y\) in two lines → frameworks fuse the two into cross_entropy on logits → no tiny \(p\) to underflow: logits \(\times 50\) in float32 give \(\infty\) and NaN separately, 119.8952 and \([0,\allowbreak\ 0,\allowbreak\ 0,\allowbreak\ -1,\allowbreak\ 1]\) fused
elevated: Every entry of \(p - y\) lies between −1 and 1 → the gradient on the logits can't blow up however big the loss is → but a confidently wrong row gets at most a push of 1 per logit, however large the gap
The \(5 \times 5\) Jacobian never has to be built → at Qwen scale that would be \(151{,}936 \times 151{,}936\) per row → \(p - y\) is one subtraction per entry
reference: Shapes: \(z\), \(p\), \(Y\) and \(dz\) are all \(3 \times 5\); \(L\) is one number
Jacobian \(J = \operatorname{diag}(p) - p^\top p\); the on row for position 2 is \([-0.0072,\allowbreak\ -0.0026,\allowbreak\ -0.0031,\allowbreak\ 0.0628,\allowbreak\ -0.0498]\)

compress.prompt: From memory, derive \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}\) for one row of the tiny model in 3–5 sentences, naming the two chain-rule pieces and what cancels. Or redraw the chain: Jacobian row → \(\times (-1/p)\) → \(p - y\) → ÷ 3, with row 2's numbers.
checklist: the loss for a row is \(-\ln p[t, y_t]\), and \(p\) depends on all five logits
softmax's Jacobian is \(\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j)\)
\(-\ln\) has slope \(-1/p\), which cancels the \(p\) in the Jacobian
the result is \(p - y\), then ÷ 3 because the loss is a mean over 3 positions

retrieve.q: Explain in plain words what each entry of \(dz[2]\) tells a training step to do, and why the sizes come out as they do.
answer: a step moves each logit against its gradient
the right word on is raised, by \(1 - p = 0.9327\) before ÷ 3
each wrong word is lowered by its own share, so mat (0.7404) most
a word already given \(p = 1\) would get 0: nothing left to fix

retrieve.q: Walk through the chain rule for \(z_{\text{mat}}\) at position 2, with the numbers, from \(L_2\) back to the logit.
answer: \(L_2 = -\ln p_{\text{on}}\), so \(\frac{\partial L_2}{\partial p_{\text{on}}} = -1/0.0673 = -14.8579\)
\(\frac{\partial p_{\text{on}}}{\partial z_{\text{mat}}} = p_{\text{on}}(0 - p_{\text{mat}}) = -0.0673 \cdot 0.7404 = -0.0498\)
multiply: the 0.0673s cancel, leaving \(0.7404 = p_{\text{mat}} - y_{\text{mat}}\)
÷ 3 for the mean gives 0.2468

retrieve.q: A teammate writes loss = -torch.log(torch.softmax(z, -1)[range(T), y]).mean() instead of F.cross_entropy(z, y). What's the same, what can break, and when would you notice?
answer: the math and, for small logits, the numbers are identical
the separate route forms \(p\), which can underflow to 0 in float32
with row 2's logits \(\times 50\): \(p_{\text{on}} = 0\), loss \(\infty\), every gradient nan
you'd notice only once logits get large, often mid-training, when one bad step ruins the weights

retrieve.q: Why must each row of \(dz\) sum to 0? Give two separate arguments.
answer: algebra: \(p\) sums to 1 and one-hot \(y\) sums to 1, so \(p - y\) sums to 0
invariance: adding a constant to every logit leaves softmax unchanged, so the loss has zero slope in that direction
measured: adding 1.0 to row 2 changed the loss by \(0.0\)

compare.q: The last card compared \(-\ln p\) with \(1 - p\) as losses. Using this card's derivation, explain why only \(-\ln\) gives a clean \(p - y\), and what \(1 - p\)'s gradient looks like instead.
answer: \(-\ln\)'s slope \(-1/p\) cancels softmax's \(p_y\) factor; \(1 - p\)'s slope is \(-1\), so nothing cancels
\(1 - p\) leaves \(-p_y(\delta_{yj} - p_j)\): the full Jacobian row
on the right logit at position 2: \(-0.9327\) for \(-\ln\) vs \(-0.0628\) for \(1 - p\)
\(1 - p\) goes quiet exactly when the model is most wrong

compare.q: Attention also runs softmax, but no log follows it. What does that change about its backward pass compared with this card?
answer: here the log cancels softmax's Jacobian; in attention nothing cancels
attention needs the full softmax backward per row: \(dS = A \odot (dA - \textstyle\sum dA \odot A)\)
both still give rows that add to 0, because softmax ignores a shift
this card's gradient is bounded by ±1; attention's depends on what flows in from above

compare.q: That card derives the same softmax − one-hot result over a batch of 32. What changes between the two derivations, and what stays the same?
answer: the same cancellation of log and exp gives \(p - y\) in both
the divisor is the number of rows in the mean: 3 here, the batch size there
both check the analytic gradient against autograd
the vocabulary width differs, the formula doesn't

predict.q: Suppose the loss used the sum over the 3 positions instead of the mean. Before computing, what would \(dz[2]\) be, and would the direction of a training step change?
predict.answer: \(dz[2]\) would be \(p - y\) itself, \([0.1076,\allowbreak\ 0.0384,\allowbreak\ 0.0464,\allowbreak\ -0.9327,\allowbreak\ 0.7404]\), three times bigger. The direction is the same; only the size changes, which acts like a learning rate three times larger.
